title: My Daily Brief
overview: This edition is led by the fallout from Friday's nationwide FAA ground stop, with Trump and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy pressing Congress for more air traffic control money while Democrats push back. The Nvidia leadership crisis continues, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent calling for a shakeup and Megaspeed launching an internal probe, and Estonia announces it will close its Russian border crossings after a foiled sabotage attempt. Also covered: an AI-assisted exam cheating scandal in South Korea, a Korean actor's drunk-driving crash, and Charlotte local news.

stories.headline: Trump comments on FAA ground stop two days later, blames Biden administration and seeks more funding
stories.summary: President Trump made his first public comments Sunday on Friday's nationwide FAA ground stop, which lasted more than four hours and led to thousands of cancellations and delays. In Truth Social posts he blamed the Biden administration for making an "old and broken" system worse and urged Congress to provide modernization money "FAST!" Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said officials are analyzing two recently installed routers at FAA facilities in Arkansas and Texas, and that the root cause is still undetermined. Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of a cyberattack.
key_facts: The ground stop began at 3:54 p.m. ET Friday, Nov. 13, and lasted more than four hours; about 3,500 flights were in the air.
The FAA said its equipment became unstable after a high volume of data flooded its network; contractor work at one site may be related.
Congress approved $12.5 billion for the FAA last year; Duffy calls it a down payment on a broader overhaul.
Biden's infrastructure law set aside $25 billion for FAA airport and air traffic control improvements, according to the agency.
Previous nationwide ground stops followed the Sept. 11 attacks and a January 2023 computer outage.

perspectives.framing: PBS/AP highlighted that Trump was "conspicuously quiet" for two days while posting about unrelated matters, and noted the $25 billion the Biden-era infrastructure law provided to the FAA, alongside Duffy's push to find the root cause.
CNBC led with Trump's blame of Biden and call for funding, and added context on prior funding, the FAA's technical explanation and the rarity of nationwide ground stops.

Fox News gave a detailed timeline emphasizing the federal response, the security review that found no signs of a cyberattack, and the White House's credit to Trump's leadership, plus disruption to college football teams. The Washington Examiner focused on Duffy saying there was no indication of a hack and describing a "whole-of-government" response led by Trump.

disputed: The root cause remains under investigation; routers in Arkansas and Texas and contractor work are being examined.
Trump's claim that the Biden administration worsened the system is contested by outlets noting Biden-era FAA funding.
The White House credits Trump's leadership for the speed of the recovery; critics note his two-day silence.
stories.why: The outage exposed how vulnerable the national air traffic system is and is shaping a funding fight in Congress.

stories.headline: Bessent urges Nvidia to pick an outside CEO and questions its China-linked sales
stories.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday on Fox News that Nvidia needs a "dramatic shakeup" after CEO Jensen Huang's resignation and should hire an outsider. He questioned whether the company pursued "seemingly illicit sales" to boost earnings, citing a fall in China sales and a rise in Singapore revenue, and demanded answers from the board within 10 days. His remarks come amid a public dispute with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over why Megaspeed was not added to the export blacklist. House Intelligence Chair Rick Crawford said it is "premature" to blame Lutnick.
key_facts: Huang resigned Thursday; CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO.
Nvidia's board says it will consider internal and external candidates; the FT reported the board approached Arm CEO Rene Haas.
Bessent said several agencies favored blacklisting Megaspeed for months, "but Commerce has the pen."
Axios reports Nvidia shares have lost more than $1.2 trillion in market value since the scandal broke in late October.
Nvidia stopped separately reporting Singapore revenue in November 2025, citing a new methodology.

perspectives.framing: CNBC and Axios focused on Bessent's questioning of Nvidia's earnings quality and the Bessent-Lutnick feud, including Cantor Fitzgerald's ties to Nvidia partners and Commerce's denial of a reported confrontation; Axios stressed market risk. The Hill featured a Republican defense of Lutnick.

Fox Business emphasized Bessent's call for an outside CEO, his claim about Singapore shell companies, Huang's alleged relationships, and the CEO search including the Haas report; it did not dwell on the Lutnick feud.

disputed: Whether Nvidia knowingly made illicit sales is unproven; Bessent framed it as a question.
Bessent's cited figure that only 1% of chips sold in Singapore stayed there comes from unspecified reporting.
Commerce denies Axios's report of a Situation Room confrontation.
CNBC notes there is no evidence Lutnick shared sensitive information with his sons or that Cantor traded on it.
stories.why: Nvidia is central to the AI economy and US growth, and a cabinet-level challenge to its leadership and finances could affect markets and export policy.

stories.headline: Top scorer on South Korea's tax accountant exam admits using AI to cheat
stories.summary: Han Won-seok, 34, who ranked first on this year's certified tax accountant exam, admitted in a video on his lawyer's YouTube channel that he cheated in both rounds using a miniature camera, generative AI and a smartphone. He said he submitted a written confession to Seoul police, who have assigned investigators, and that he used the same method on a CPA exam. The presidential office ordered a full investigation into suspected AI cheating across national certification tests, days before Thursday's college entrance exam. Officials are moving to invalidate his result, and the exam administrator is considering a criminal complaint.
key_facts: He scored 397.5 out of 400 in the April first round, missing one of 160 questions.
Two proctors were assigned to his exam room, per the exam administrator.
Cheaters face invalidation and a five-year ban from the exam.
Prime Minister Han Seong-sook is to meet ministry officials Monday on prevention measures.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian stressed that his scores looked too good to be true, his earlier denials, and the role of standardized tests in South Korean social mobility, ahead of the college exam.

Yonhap, BBC and the Korea Herald gave detailed accounts of the method, scores, government response and penalties; the BBC noted his stated motives and remorse, and the Korea Herald highlighted that he cheated in front of two proctors.

disputed: Whether criminal charges will follow depends on the police investigation.
How widespread AI cheating is on other national exams is unknown pending the government review.
stories.why: It shows how generative AI is challenging the integrity of high-stakes exams, just before South Korea's national college entrance test.

stories.headline: Duffy blames past administrations and Congress for ground stop; Van Hollen pushes back
stories.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday on CNN that prior administrations and insufficient congressional funding left the air traffic system vulnerable, saying the $12.5 billion approved last year cannot fund new telecom architecture, software or towers. He said botched routine maintenance by a contractor, replacing copper lines with fiber optic, triggered the stoppage, and that the root cause is still being investigated. Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) said it was "really rich" to blame Congress when it gave the administration what it requested, but said he would support whatever money is necessary on a bipartisan basis. Duffy defended Trump's two-day delay in commenting, saying the president was fully engaged.
key_facts: Duffy: "I take responsibility for what was given to me by prior administrations."
The contractor, L3Harris, is reportedly running diagnostics.
Van Hollen: "I will support whatever level of money is necessary to fix this problem."

perspectives.framing: The Guardian framed it as the administration shifting blame, giving weight to Van Hollen's criticism and Trump's delayed response while including Duffy's detailed explanation of funding limits.
The Hill led with Duffy blaming predecessors and Congress for underfunding.
The Washington Examiner led with Van Hollen pledging bipartisan funding, while noting he rejected Duffy's blame.

disputed: Whether existing funds have been adequately spent, as Van Hollen suggests, or are insufficient in scope, as Duffy says.
The precise cause of the maintenance failure is still under investigation.
stories.why: The blame dispute will shape whether and how quickly Congress funds air traffic control upgrades.

stories.headline: Rollover crash briefly closes I-77 northbound in Huntersville
stories.summary: A rollover crash just after noon Sunday on I-77 northbound before Exit 23 near Gilead Road in Huntersville closed all northbound lanes. Medic said one person was taken to a hospital with serious injuries; Huntersville Fire said two people were treated. Lanes reopened around 2:20 p.m. The cause is under investigation.
key_facts: Crash occurred around noon Sunday, Nov. 15, near Exit 23 (Gilead Road).
One person hospitalized with serious injuries.
Northbound lanes reopened around 2:20 p.m.

perspectives.framing: All four local stations reported it as a straightforward traffic incident, focusing on injuries and lane closures.

disputed: The cause of the crash and the injured person's condition were not reported.
stories.why: It affected a major commuter route north of Charlotte.

stories.headline: Analyst says Jensen Huang will not return to Nvidia despite reported comeback push
stories.summary: The Financial Times reported that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has discussed returning, with allies organizing a "war room" of tech executives to lobby the board and seek White House backing. Wedbush-turned-Yorkville analyst Dan Ives told Newsweek he sees "no chance" of a return, suggesting outside candidates such as Tim Cook or Nikesh Arora. A Verge newsletter traced the scandal from an Oct. 29 New York Times report on a suspected Chinese spy plot to Huang's admission of an affair and his resignation.
key_facts: Huang resigned Thursday after 33 years leading the company he co-founded.
Nvidia's board is investigating the conduct that led to his resignation.
China has denied the espionage allegations; Nvidia previously said it had no reason to believe security or secrets were compromised.

perspectives.framing: The Verge offered a timeline emphasizing national security stakes, Huang's push to loosen export restrictions, and his closeness to Trump, while noting disagreement among US intelligence officials on the evidence.
Newsweek centered on investor and analyst views about a possible comeback and succession, quoting Ives and a governance expert.

disputed: Whether Huang is actually seeking a return rests on anonymous sources.
US intelligence officials reportedly disagree over the strength of evidence linking Alice Huang to Beijing.
Ives's speculation about a new company or SpaceX role is unconfirmed.
stories.why: Nvidia's leadership future affects the AI industry and a large share of US market value.

stories.headline: Estonia to close road border crossings with Russia after foiled attack on drone maker
stories.summary: Estonia will close its border crossings with Russia from Dec. 1 after what authorities say was a GRU-ordered attempt to bomb and burn drone maker Threod Systems near Tallinn on Saturday. Security staff and police intervened; eight suspects, reportedly from Latvia, were detained, and custody is being sought for five. Prime Minister Kristen Michal called it part of Russia's hybrid war to weaken support for Ukraine. Russia's foreign ministry spokeswoman called the border plan "aggressive and unrestrained Russophobia."
key_facts: Closure takes effect Dec. 1; its duration was not specified.
Estonia has three crossings with Russia: Narva, Koidula and Luhamaa.
Estonia attributed an August arson attack on Milrem Robotics to Russian intelligence; the Kremlin denied it.
No injuries were reported.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian and Al Jazeera emphasized Estonian officials' framing of a Russian shadow war, included Russia's Russophobia response, and Al Jazeera added Latvian and parliamentary voices urging asymmetric responses.
Newsweek and DW reported the official Estonian statements, with Newsweek adding context on Estonian history and recent US-mediated Russia-Ukraine talks.

The New York Post framed it as a NATO ally foiling a Russian plot, highlighting that the suspects came from Latvia and KAPO's warning against Russian 'job offers'; it said Russia had not immediately commented.

disputed: Estonia says it has clear evidence of GRU involvement; Russia rejects such accusations.
Outlets differ on whether all crossings or only road crossings will close.
stories.why: A NATO member sealing its border with Russia marks an escalation in Europe's response to alleged Russian sabotage.

stories.headline: Megaspeed says Alice Huang left in 2025 and launches internal probe
stories.summary: Singapore-based Megaspeed, the largest buyer of Nvidia chips in Southeast Asia, said Alice Huang left the company effective Aug. 30, 2025, and that it has hired outside lawyers for an internal investigation. The company said reports about its business and supply chain are "not supported by verifiable evidence" and that it complies with US export controls. It is suspected of giving Chinese companies access to Nvidia chips through data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand. Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month.
key_facts: Singapore began investigating Megaspeed in February 2025, including possible false declarations on server purchases.
Singapore found insufficient evidence that Alice Huang committed a crime.
Bessent said whether she is a spy "doesn't matter to me"; his focus is Nvidia's compliance culture.
China denies Alice Huang is a spy.

perspectives.framing: PBS/AP focused on Megaspeed's statement, Singapore's investigation history and Bessent's comments on Nvidia's culture.
The BBC covered the same statement, adding the Bessent-Lutnick dispute, congressional scrutiny, Singapore's position on foreign export controls, and China's warning against a technological blockade.

disputed: Whether Megaspeed diverted chips to China is alleged but unproven.
Whether Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset is disputed.
stories.why: The case tests how well US export controls on advanced AI chips can be enforced abroad.

stories.headline: Actor Ko Kyung-pyo apologizes for drunk-driving crash and suspends work
stories.summary: South Korean actor Ko Kyung-pyo, 36, apologized on Instagram after crashing into a district cleaning truck while drunk around 3:30 a.m. Saturday in Seoul's Mapo district. Police said his blood alcohol exceeded the 0.08% license-revocation threshold; a truck driver in his 60s was slightly injured. Ko said he will suspend activities and cooperate with police, and addressed questions about footage of him pocketing an object, which he said was his car key. Several shows are editing out his appearances.
key_facts: Crash occurred around 3:30 a.m. Saturday in Donggyo-dong, Mapo-gu.
His exact blood alcohol level was not disclosed.
Fan meetings scheduled for next Saturday were canceled.

perspectives.framing: The Korea Herald and Yonhap reported his apology and the production fallout; the Herald addressed the surveillance-footage controversy and why he drove on after the collision.

disputed: Online speculation about what he pocketed; he says it was his car key.
stories.why: It is a prominent case of celebrity drunk driving with immediate effects on Korean TV productions.

stories.headline: Charlotte stays sunny and chilly before warming this week
stories.summary: Charlotte saw a sunny but cold Sunday with highs struggling to reach the mid-50s. Patchy frost is likely Monday morning, with lows near or below freezing. Afternoons warm to the 60s midweek and near 70 by Friday, with little chance of needed rain.
key_facts: Lows in the 20s and 30s Monday morning.
Highs near 70 expected Friday and the weekend.
Little rain is forecast.

perspectives.framing: Local stations gave a routine forecast, noting the dry pattern.

stories.why: Frost and dry conditions may affect commutes, plants and outdoor plans.

investigations.question: What is happening with AI regulation in the US and EU?
investigations.update: No articles in this edition address AI regulation in the US or EU. Related coverage concerns US export controls on Nvidia AI chips and South Korea's response to AI-assisted exam cheating, but neither covers AI regulation as such.
